## Discord Question-Thread Findings (DQ ledger)

*Source: **DQ** = Discord question thread. DQ-1 … DQ-6 from the thread posted 2026-07-09 through 2026-07-15; RJ's substantive replies are dated 2026-07-09. Numbering continues unbroken from the established source-tag series. Same ledger discipline as the IP block above: each entry carries an anchor pointer rather than being folded into the section body.*

**DQ-1.** [Stated] Anchor: §Formularies / OQ formulary-authority (GATING for Bucket A) — **Formulary self-contradictions, enumerated.** Asked to list the self-contradictions he sees in the Thirty-Nine Articles and any exceptions he takes, RJ answered (Discord, 2026-07-09, 4:46 PM) that the tensions are "amongst the whole of the Formularies: the Prayer Book, the Articles, and the Books of Homilies," and "are not so clearly evident apart from their context." **Instance 1:** "The more Lutheran understanding of the Sacrament is seen in the Liturgy, Catechism, and some aspects of the Homilies, and the more explicitly Calvinist understanding is seen mostly in the last Article inserted: Article XXIX (inserted in 1571, after excommunication by the Bishop of Rome)." He adds the history: Article XXIX "was actually controversial in its day; the more Reformed party had tried to insert it earlier in 1563, but it was removed. When it was reinserted in 1571, it was done so at the opposition of Bishop Edmund Guest and others." **Instance 2:** "Article VI's understanding of the Apocrypha with the Books of Homilies constant reference to the Apocrypha." Article VI "maintains a purposefully ambiguous state for the Apocrypha, stating that the Books therein cannot be cited alone to support doctrinal claims, but not outright denying their (at least Deuterocanonical) canonicity," while the Homilies "freely reference them (always with Protocanonical Texts), using terms like, 'the Holy Ghost Spake in Tobit, saying.'" He offered exact examples once he has his physical copy to hand. **Addendum (5:49 PM):** the formularies "were made over the course of a century" (Prayer Book earliest aspects 1544, full 1549, official 1662; Homilies c.1540s-1570s; Articles 1550s-1570s), i.e. "over one century of development."

> **[Analysis] GATE RESULT (this is the load-bearing consequence).** The enumeration is confined to **sacramentology and canon**. Neither instance touches worship regulation. Articles 20 and 34, and the worship-related Homilies (esp. "Against the Peril of Idolatry"), **pass through the self-contradictions hedge ungated**. The Bucket A worship levers remain available. This substantially answers half of the long-standing formulary-authority open question; see the OQ block above, now updated.
>
> **[Analysis]** The century-of-development addendum is his *explanation for why tension is tolerable*, not an expansion of the enumeration. Note also that **the exceptions half of the question went unanswered** — he listed tensions only. That half remains open, and the posted closure question (Question List v12) is aimed at locking the enumeration.
>
> **[Analysis] Attribution guard.** Nothing here converts the formularies into a standard RJ calls *binding*. RC1-7 (explicit denial of juridical subscription) and GV-37 (1662 BCP named as the benchmark prayer books "are supposed to conform theologically to") continue to govern the framing: *your formularies / what you affirm / the standard you name*.

**DQ-2.** [Stated] Anchor: §6 (Sacraments — Number & Definition) ; cross-ref IP-4, GV-24/39, Q7 — **Article 25 and the seven sacraments.** RJ (Discord, 2026-07-09): "We separate them by pointing to the two as Dominical/Gospel, as their Signs are given/commanded directly by our Lord, and pertain to the Forgiveness of sins, and the Five Ecclesial Sacraments as developing from the Life of the Church, rooted in Apostolic Tradition. The Five are not of the same level and kind as the Two. The Five can be called 'Sacraments', so long as they are not seen as Sacraments of the Gospel." He grounds this in the Second Book of Homilies, "Common Prayer and Sacraments Ought to Be Ministered in a Tongue That is Understanded of the Hearers," quoting it at length, including its statements that on the exact signification "there be but two, namely, Baptism, and the Supper of the Lord"; that "in a general acception the name of a Sacrament may be attributed to any thing whereby an holy thing is signified," a class the Homily extends to "oil, washing of feet, and such like"; and that the other rites retained by the Church of England are to be taken "either for godly states of life… or else judged to be such ordinances as may make for the instruction, comfort, and edification of Christ's Church."

> **[Analysis] RETIRE THE LEVER.** This is a formulary-faithful answer. The Article 25 lever moves to the do-not-deploy register alongside Lent and baptismal regeneration (Question List v12).
>
> **[Analysis] Two residues worth logging.** First, **the grace half of the question was not answered**: whether the Five *confer grace* is untouched, and that is where the Roman difference actually lives (Trent: seven, all conferring grace *ex opere operato*, all instituted by Christ). His answer is compatible with "the Five confer grace, just not the forgiveness tied to a Dominical sign." Second, there is a gap between the Homily's deflationary "general acception" (a class covering foot-washing and oil) and his capitalized "Ecclesial Sacraments… developing from the Life of the Church, rooted in Apostolic Tradition," which is a **positive dogmatic category the Homily does not supply**. Staged as a soft follow-up (Question List v12, Bucket C).
>
> **[Analysis] METHOD DATUM (raises the value of Homily-based material generally).** He treats the Homilies as his **authoritative interpretive lens on the Articles**. This lifts the standing of every Homily-anchored lever in the project, including "Against the Peril of Idolatry" (§12, Q2, QC-b).

**DQ-3.** [Stated] Anchor: §13 (Worship Theology & the Regulative Principle) / OQ8 ; cross-ref IP-2, BP-41 — **RPW "rightly understood": the five-example answer.** Asked where the typical confessional understanding of the RPW gets it wrong and what he would correct, RJ (Discord, 2026-07-09, 5:20 PM) defined "the most extreme I can think of" (exclusive Psalms, required a capella, no images/crosses, no worship except Sundays, no Feast Days including Christmas and Easter, no recitation of Creeds) and refuted it in five numbered points:
>
> 1. "Psalms are not exclusively required. Matthew 26:30 shows our Lord and the Apostles singing an hymn together."
> 2. "A capella is not required. Psalm 150 makes little sense in light of the fact that it lists all sorts of instruments for praise. The counter to this is that praise is not the same as worship. **The problem is that praise is an element of worship**, and the Psalm (and the rest of Scripture) does not say, 'Praise Him with these instruments, unless it's in the form of worship.'"
> 3. "Images are all throughout the worship of the Old Testament, and even commanded by God, from the bronze serpent (Numbers 21:4-9) to the Temple itself (1 Kings 6; 2 Chronicles 3), to the Ark of the Covenant." Cherubim on the ark (Exod 25:18-22); Joshua and the elders "rightly bowed down before the Ark" (Josh 7:6); the ark as "the footstool of our God" (1 Chron 28:2); bowing before the footstool (Ps 99:5; 132:7-8). "We are not to bow to the images in the sense of obeisance to them, but to the untrained eye seeing Joshua and the Elders bow before the Presence of the Lord at the Ark would look like bowing to the images of the Cherubim."
> 4. Not Sunday-only: daily gathering (Acts 2:46-47); apostolic temple worship (Acts 3:1) and synagogue attendance (Acts 13:14-15; 17:1-3); and "Christ Himself participated in 'extrabiblical' Feast Days: namely, He participated in the Feast of Dedication, Hannukah, which comes from 1 Maccabees 4:52-59 (this is found in John 10:22-23). So according to the Biblical witness, **Feast Days can be added to the Calendar apart from Divine Command**."
> 5. On creeds: opposing recitation because "the exact word-order is not directly found in Scripture would be like opposing a homily or a prayer because the exact word-order is not directly found in Scripture." Notes the early Puritan petition to King James VI and I opposing the Canticles (Nunc Dimittis, Magnificat, Benedictus) for not being Psalms.

> **[Stated-Analysis]** He did not engage the mainstream three-bucket Westminster version, and **did not state a positive rule of his own**. The answer is a refutation of a caricature.
>
> **[Analysis] ELEMENT VOCABULARY — standing attribution rule updated.** Point 2 is the **first logged instance of RJ using "element" as a term of art**: "praise is an element of worship." He demonstrably speaks the taxonomy. **He has still never applied "element" to incense**; that classification remains **project Analysis**, not Stated. The rule changes only in this respect: it is no longer available to say he does not use the vocabulary.
>
> **[Analysis] METHOD FINDING (high value).** **Four of the five rebuttals argue from POSITIVE WARRANT.** Hymns by dominical example (Matt 26:30). Instruments by command (Ps 150). Images by command (bronze serpent, cherubim, temple). Creeds by necessary-inference-style reasoning (forms of commanded acts). Only point 4's Hanukkah move argues from permission. This is **the confessional RPW method deployed by RJ himself**, and it licenses posing the incense question in his own idiom: "you defended images by pointing to where God commanded them; where is incense commanded, and what did the command regulate?"
>
> **[Analysis] His targets are largely not Westminster positions.** WCF 21.5 provides for solemn fastings and thanksgivings on special occasions, so "Sunday-only" is not the confessional view; confessional Presbyterians recite creeds and sing composed hymns as *forms* of commanded elements; JD's own position already allows instruments and newly composed hymns. **His stated corrections leave the version of the RPW used in the incense argument untouched.**
>
> **[Analysis] HANUKKAH MOVE.** "Feast Days can be added to the Calendar apart from Divine Command" is his **one genuinely normative-principle argument**. Limits: (i) attendance at a national commemoration is not *institution* of a worship element; (ii) it licenses at most uncommanded *calendar observances*, which is Lent / Article 34 territory and uncontested by the incense argument; (iii) **it cannot reach incense**, because on his own account incense is COMMANDED (Mal 1:11) and is a Godward offering. A commanded offering cannot simultaneously shelter as an optional human addition. **His own warrant claim closes the Hanukkah door for incense.** Same fork as the dual-warrant tension (see `RJ_Incense_Analysis.md`).
>
> **[Analysis]** His Acts 3:1 / synagogue datum is pre-answered by the **overlap-period** concept (see `RJ_Incense_Analysis.md`, new section): tolerated Jewish-Christian temple piety during AD 30-70, in an economy Hebrews 8:13 pronounces obsolete and "ready to vanish away," is not a warrant for importing temple ceremonial into Gentile worship — precisely what the Jerusalem council declined to do (Acts 15).

**DQ-4.** [Stated] ★★ (highest-value item in this batch) Anchor: §13 / OQ8 ; **closes the definitional gate open since IP-2** — **THE WARRANT AFFIRMATION.** JD posted (Discord, 2026-07-09/10), in substance: the extreme examples are not the RPW itself but the strictest applications found in some traditions; WCF 21.5 provides for occasional fastings and thanksgivings; creeds and composed hymns are varying *forms* of existing commanded acts, not new *types* of acts of worship. Then: "One thing I noticed is the method you used in the examples you gave: you see warrant for the use of hymns from Christ's example, instruments from Psalm 150's command, and images from God's command for the serpent and the cherubim. In each case the practice is defended by pointing to positive warrant in Scripture, whether command, approved example, or necessary inference. That's the regulative principle as I understand it. Is that the regulative principle you hold ('rightly understood'): that acts of worship require positive warrant in Scripture, whether by command, approved example, or necessary inference? If not, what's the third option between 'needs positive warrant' and 'permitted unless forbidden'?"
>
> RJ's reply, **verbatim**: "Correct; this is why I will sometimes say that I do hold to the RPW, but just rightly applied (with as little snark as possible!). One of the fundamental issues I see with the way the RPW is used today is how Old Testament examples aren't allowed, and often even Revelation is not allowed. I one time knew a man who held to the RPW, but in a 'contemporary worship' sort of way. His position was that liturgical worship of anything more formal than a non-denominational worship service was a violation of Scripture's principles for worship. When I would point to the Old Testament, he would say I couldn't do that. When I would point to Revelation, he would say that's in Heaven so we can't do that yet. He was a strange beast, indeed."

> **[Stated]** RJ **affirms** ("Correct") the principle as restated: **acts of worship require positive warrant in Scripture, whether by command, approved example, or necessary inference.** This closes the definitional gate open since IP-2 and answers the element/circumstance-adjacent OQ at the level that matters (the warrant rule itself; the element/circumstance *line* is still undrawn by him — see the OQ block above).
>
> **[Stated] Vocabulary shift:** "rightly **applied**" replaces "rightly understood." He now positions himself as holding **the same principle** with different applications, not a different principle.
>
> **[Stated] His positive distinctive, stated as a general rule for the first time:** the fundamental issue he sees is that "Old Testament examples aren't allowed, and often even Revelation is not allowed" as warrant sources. Full position: **warrant required; warrant sources include OT commands/examples and Revelation's heavenly worship.**
>
> **[Analysis] STRATEGIC EFFECT.** Every subsequent question is now an intramural **application** question under a **shared rule**. This is the friendliest possible ground and the on-ramp the incense funnel has waited for since IP-2.
>
> **[Analysis] Do not contest the expanded warrant sources in the abstract.** In the abstract he is right, and the Reformed tradition argues from the OT constantly (Lord's Day from creation and the fourth commandment; covenantal paedobaptism). The real rule is not "no OT examples" but **"OT warrant transfers unless it belonged to the fulfilled ceremonial economy"** — a FILTER, not a wall. The entire remaining incense dispute is now: **what is the filter on OT and Revelation warrant?**
>
> **[Analysis]** His OT warrants to date (cherubim, temple images, instruments) share a feature: **none was priesthood-restricted or given an explicit NT antitype**. Incense differs in kind: priesthood-restricted on pain of death, sanctuary-located, compound-specified, and explicitly interpreted by Rev 5:8. **The filter question exposes the difference; the abstract sources question hides it.**

**DQ-6.** [EXT / third-party, Discord — **not RJ**] Anchor: §13 / §14 (conservative-retention default) ; cross-ref BP-59 — **The Laud quotation.** A third participant (handle **M1B3AU**, self-described as between Anglo-Catholic and Reformed, "leaning more towards the Anglo-Catholic side") posted in RJ's self-contradictions thread (2026-07-10) a quotation **attributed** to Archbishop Laud: "…I would have them remember that we live in a Church reformed, not in one made new. > **[Analysis] For the record (left uncorrected in-thread by design; thread energy preserved for the RJ funnel).** M1B3AU's accompanying historical claims are substantially inaccurate. The Westminster Assembly was called by the **English** Parliament and met in London (Jerusalem Chamber, Westminster Abbey) to reform the **English** church, with Scottish commissioners joining after the Solemn League and Covenant; it did not convene in Scotland and its purpose was not Scottish separation from England. "Plagiarizes Calvin and Zwingli" is confused: the WCF's sacramentology is Calvinist, **not** Zwinglian. The "Articles as unity document vs WCF/LBCF as separation documents" framing is spin: the Articles were an instrument of **state uniformity** with enforced subscription and deprivations for nonconformity.

**DQ-7.** [Stated + Analysis] ★ Anchor: §13 (Worship Theology & the Regulative Principle) / OQ8 ; cross-ref DQ-4, DQ-5, IP-2, Rev-9/10/11 — **THE APPROVED-EXAMPLE FILTER, AND THE UNGROUNDED "OF NECESSITY" MODAL.** In the RPW thread (Discord, **2026-07-21, 11:42 AM** — *date corrected 260724-1 from the archived thread; previously logged as 07-22, which was the intake date*), RJ stated, in his own words, the filter by which a scriptural example transfers: an example **"lauded or not treated as sinful"** would mean we **"of necessity have to find it appropriate."**

> **[Stated]** This is the **first stated transfer rule for the Revelation strand** of the warrant question in any logged source. Its structure: *depiction in an approved — or merely uncondemned — scriptural scene generates an obligation to treat the practice as appropriate for worship today.*
>
> **⚠️ [Analysis — BUCKET A, internal consistency. The load-bearing finding in this entry.]** The disjunct **"or not treated as sinful"** is **normative-principle reasoning**: *absence of condemnation functioning as warrant.* That stands in direct tension with **DQ-4**, where he affirmed ("Correct") that acts of worship require **positive warrant** by command, approved example, or necessary inference. Note precisely where the seam is: **"lauded" sits inside the DQ-4 rule** — that is what an *approved* example is. **"Not treated as sinful" sits outside it.** It is the "permitted unless forbidden" half of the very fork DQ-4 asked him to choose between, reappearing inside his own filter as an *alternative sufficient condition*. **This is intramural, not cross-tradition:** it requires no contested Reformed premise, only his own two statements laid side by side. Frame it as a clarification, never as a gotcha: *"Does the second half do independent work — is an uncondemned example enough on its own, or does it need to be an approved one?"* The friendly form is also the strongest form here, because the likeliest honest answer is that he did not intend the disjunct to carry weight, and that answer costs him the Revelation-strand warrant for incense without anyone having to charge him with inconsistency.
>
> **⚠️ [Analysis] THE "OF NECESSITY" MODAL IS ASSERTED, NOT GROUNDED.** He states that such an example means we *of necessity* have to find the practice appropriate. **He has not explained why depiction generates necessity.** Depiction of a practice within a scene is not, on its face, institution of that practice for the gathered church — and the modal is carrying the entire load with no stated basis under it. **This is the open seam in the Revelation strand: the answer is on the record; the reason for it is not.** The next move on this strand is to ask for the ground, not to contest the rule — asking why depiction obligates is a genuine question, and it is the question his own formulation invites.
>
> **[Stated — COMMON GROUND. Record as such; do NOT deploy as a lever.]** In the same exchange RJ stated his position on invocation: **asking God to have the saints in heaven pray for us**, which he holds is unobjectionable, and which he attributes to **Trent Horn's formulation** (attribution per RJ's own claim; not independently verified — see flag below). This is **compatible with Article 22**, whose condemnation is of the Romish doctrine of the *invocation of saints* — address directed **to** the saints — not of asking God that others pray. It also **narrows rather than contradicts** his earlier datum ("I do not find a principle in Scripture that would allow for prayers to the Saints"): he is declining direct address while retaining a mediated form. **Logged as common ground. Not a lever, and not to be used as one** — attempting it would spend goodwill on a position his own formularies permit.
>
> **⚠️ [FLAG — two items to verify before any deployment.]** (1) The verbatim fragments above are **as relayed from the live thread**, not yet checked against the archived post text; re-verify against the Discord post itself before deployment, per the standing quote-precision rule. (2) The Trent Horn attribution as logged here reads *RJ credits the formulation to Horn.* If the intended sense was the reverse — RJ claiming to be the original source Horn drew from — **correct this line at the next pass.** The two are materially different claims and must not sit ambiguous in the ledger.

**DQ-8.** [Stated] ★★ Anchor: §13 / OQ8 ; **answers DQ-5** ; cross-ref DQ-4, DQ-9, IP-3, Rev-9/10/11 — **THE OT-CARRYOVER FILTER, ANSWERED.** Twenty minutes after JD posted the crux question, RJ replied (Discord, **2026-07-10, 11:06 PM**), verbatim and in full:

> *"By looking at what we have received as the consensus-form of worship, and comparing it to what we see espoused in Scripture. For instance, we do have the Passover Lamb as central to our worship. Christ is also our priest. Both of these are strongly in the New Testament."*

> **[Stated]** His filter is **two-stage**: (i) *the received consensus-form of worship* supplies the candidate practice; (ii) *comparison with what Scripture espouses* tests it. Worked examples given: the **Passover Lamb**, "central to our worship," and **Christ as priest** — both, he says, "strongly in the New Testament."
>
> **[Analysis] — order of operations is the whole finding.** Under **DQ-4** (which he affirmed with "Correct") the question is *where is this warranted?*; Scripture supplies the candidate and the practice must be shown to have warrant. Under **DQ-8** the question is *is what we have received contradicted?*; tradition supplies the candidate and Scripture serves as a check on it. **These are not the same test**, and the gap between them is precisely the regulative/normative fork. This is not a gotcha and must not be run as one — it is the most natural thing in the world for a high-church pastor to say, and he plainly does not experience the two as different. But it is the seam, it is intramural, and it needs no contested Reformed premise: only his own DQ-4 answer and his own DQ-8 answer side by side.
>
> **⚠️ [Analysis] — THE HIGH-VALUE FINDING: his own two examples model fulfilment-by-antitype, not carryover.** Look at what each example actually does. The Passover Lamb is "central to our worship" **because Christ is the Passover** — the OT ceremonial act (the slaughter and eating of a literal lamb) is *not* retained; its antitype is. "Christ is also our priest" **concedes that the Levitical priesthood does not survive** — again, the antitype is retained and the OT office is not. **Neither example is a case of an Old Covenant ceremonial *act* being carried into New Covenant worship in material form.** Both are cases of a type terminating in Christ. So **his own filter, applied to his own worked examples, produces the Reformed result** — which is exactly the argument the project runs against material incense, where Rev 5:8 names the antitype (the prayers of the saints) in the text itself.
>
> **⚠️ [Analysis] — Heb 7:12 conceded in his own words.** "Christ is also our priest," offered as his own example of correct OT carryover, is the load-bearing premise of the **priesthood-mediation refinement** staged on 260723-1 (§13 entry; question list item **1e / `Q-Inc-5``**; `RJ_Incense_Analysis.md` §4.12). That refinement needed him to grant that the Levitical priesthood is fulfilled and superseded rather than continued. **He has now granted it unprompted, in a neutral context, before incense was ever mentioned.** This is the strongest single datum the funnel has acquired, and it was acquired at zero cost.
>
> **[Analysis] — do not overstate.** He has *not* said that every OT ceremonial act must terminate in an antitype, and he would not accept that as a stated rule. The finding is that **his own chosen examples exhibit that pattern**, which makes the pattern askable as a question — *"both of your examples look like cases where the Old Testament thing is fulfilled in Christ rather than continued; is that the pattern, or are there cases where the practice itself carries forward?"* — and unaskable as an allegation.

**DQ-9.** [Stated] ★★ Anchor: §13 / OQ8 ; cross-ref DQ-4, DQ-8, DQ-3, EXT-Cooper — **THE MILK-AND-HONEY REFINEMENT: "PRINCIPLES AND NOT INDIVIDUAL ACTS."** Pressed by JD (07-11, 8:14 AM) on whether a practice well established in the received consensus but absent from Scripture would pass on consensus alone, RJ answered (Discord, **2026-07-11, 8:43 AM**) with the milk-and-honey hypothetical: some early Christians gave milk and honey to the newly baptized; *supposing that became a universal tradition,* he does not believe it would violate a proper understanding of the RPW, **"because the RPW is about principles and not individual acts."** His stated complaint: others use the RPW "for individual practices, demanding those EXACT practices be found in Scripture, rather than principles that are drawn from the witness of Scripture." **His stated principle:** *"that imagery and symbolism are to reflect the Biblical witness"* — milk and honey point to the Promised Land, which ties to Baptism and to the Old Testament. His contrast, in his own words: others say *"We see no example of milk and honey being given after Baptism, therefore we must reject that"*; he says *"We see examples of imagery being tied to their fulfillment, and this act ties the imagery of the Promised Land to Baptism, so this fits that principle well."* He adds a parity argument: quoting 1 Cor 10:1-2 at a baptism is equally not found in Scripture as an individual act, and prohibiting the milk while permitting the quotation "makes no sense to me." He closes by linking **two Jordan Cooper videos** ("How Does Our Theology Affect How We Worship?"; "A Discussion on the Regulative Principle of Worship") as representative of where he is coming from.

Do not cite as support for outline Step 2b.**

Arriving from this dossier, you hit the guard first. That is the whole purpose of the pointer — do not remove it.**

> **⚠️ [Analysis] — this is the live obstacle, and it is bigger than the DQ-7 seam.** DQ-9 substantially **loosens** the DQ-4 affirmation without formally retracting it. DQ-4's three warrant sources — command, approved example, necessary inference — are all **act-level** warrants; an *approved example* is, by definition, an example of an act. DQ-9 replaces act-level warrant with **principle-level** warrant: a practice is licensed if it instantiates a principle abstracted from Scripture. **Under DQ-9, incense passes trivially** ("imagery reflecting the biblical witness," Rev 5:8, Mal 1:11) and so does virtually any ceremony in the Western tradition. **If DQ-9 is left unengaged, the entire funnel dissolves at the last step**, because every prepared incense question presupposes act-level warrant. Treat this as the primary obstacle, ahead of the DQ-7 grounding question in importance if not in sequence.

> **[Analysis] — JD's follow-up was the correct move and is already on the record.** JD's 07-11 3:48 PM reply names the problem exactly ("a test that a very wide range of practices could pass… what does the principle rule out, not just what it rules in") and asks for an excluded case. That is the right pressure and it needs no reconstruction. See **DQ-10** for what came back.
>
> **[Analysis] — the 1 Cor 10:1-2 parity argument is a category confusion, and should NOT be pressed.** Reading Scripture aloud is a commanded element (1 Tim 4:13); *which* text is read is a circumstance under that element. Introducing a new material rite is not the same kind of act. But note: **JD has already put this exact distinction on the record**, in the 07-10 1:26 PM post, in his own prior wording (creeds and composed hymns as varying *forms* of existing commanded acts, not new *types* of acts). If the point is needed later it can be re-anchored to JD's own earlier words rather than introduced as a fresh objection — which is both friendlier and harder to deflect. **Low priority; do not spend a turn on it.**

> **[Analysis] — METHOD DATUM (Bucket A relevance).** He names **Jordan Cooper**, a confessional Lutheran, as representative of his own RPW frame. This matters: **the Lutheran adiaphora frame is not the frame of Article 20 or of the Homilies.** Article 20 gives the Church power to decree rites and ceremonies but expressly denies it authority to ordain anything contrary to God's Word or to expound one place of Scripture repugnant to another; the Homilies' register on ceremonial accretion is stricter still. This is a **Bucket A observation, not a Bucket B one** — the question is not "Lutheran vs. Reformed" but "which frame do your own formularies supply?" **Stage; do not deploy in the RPW thread**, which is already carrying the funnel. Cross-ref the existing EXT-Cooper sub-tag.

**DQ-10.** [Stated] ★ Anchor: §13 / §12 ; cross-ref DQ-9, DQ-7, RC3-8, BP-38 — **THE BOUNDARY ANSWER: ONE EXCLUSION, PRODUCED BY A DIFFERENT RULE.** Asked directly (JD, 07-11 3:48 PM) for an example of a practice his imagery-and-symbolism principle would **exclude**, RJ answered (Discord, **2026-07-11, 11:22 PM**), in a single sentence: *"I do not find a principle in Scripture that would allow for prayers to the Saints, so that would be one example."* Pressed (JD, 07-12) on what specifically blocks it, he replied (**2026-07-21, 12:04 AM**) in two numbered points: **(1)** he does not see how Rev 5:8 and 8:3-4 prove that petitioning the saints directly is appropriate — "There seems to be a leap there" from *the prayers of the saints are received in Heaven as a part of the worship* to *therefore we can pray to particular Saints… in some supernatural way and that it is good to do so*; **(2)** *"What blocks my usage of prayers to the Saints in Heaven is that prayer is always seen as an act of worship and as directed to God alone."*

> **⚠️ [Analysis] — THE MOST DEPLOYABLE FINDING IN THIS BATCH.** Read point (2) carefully. **The exclusion is not produced by the imagery principle.** It is produced by an entirely separate rule about the proper *object* of worship. So when the imagery-and-symbolism principle was asked, directly and in the friendliest possible terms, to produce a single exclusion, **it produced none** — the one case offered is ruled out on other grounds and would be ruled out by anybody, on any principle, including a strict normative-principle Anglican.
>
> **The consequence, stated carefully:** a principle that licenses practices and excludes none is a **permission-generator, not a filter**. That is the normative principle under a different name — the very position RJ has explicitly declined (he called it "too loose," IP-2/DQ-3, and affirmed positive warrant at DQ-4). **Intramural; needs no Reformed premise; runs entirely on his own three answers.**
>
> **Deployment form — clarification, never charge, and the wording matters:** *"Is there anything the imagery principle itself rules out — some practice that genuinely does reflect a biblical image, but that you'd still exclude? I ask because prayers to the saints seem to be ruled out by the second thing you said, that prayer is worship and belongs to God alone, which I'd agree with, rather than by the imagery test itself. I'm trying to see what work the imagery principle is doing on its own."* This is a continuation of a question JD has already asked once, not a new line of pressure, which is what makes it natural rather than pointed.
>
> **[Analysis] — the "leap" in point (1): handle with precision, do NOT overstate.** It is tempting to read point (1) as RJ rejecting depiction-to-practice inference as such, which would be the perfect mirror of the project's incense argument. **That reading is wrong and must not be deployed.** His **DQ-7** answer ("It is the first") says the opposite: depiction of an approved or uncondemned example *does* generate obligation. His objection here is narrower and text-specific — that **Rev 5:8 does not depict prayer *to* the saints at all**, which he grounds in the genitive (see DQ-7a note below on the Greek). So the leap he names is a leap from a **misread text**, not from depiction to practice.
> The honest asymmetry that survives is narrower but still real, and it is the **self-interpreting-cluster** form already recorded at 260723-1: he reads the *same verse* as depicting incense-to-be-enacted while the verse glosses the incense as the prayers. **Route through the existing cluster question (Rev 1:20 / 4:5 / 5:8 / 19:8), not through a depiction-to-practice charge.**

**DQ-11.** [Stated] Anchor: §6 (Sacraments — Number & Definition) ; **closes question-list item 20** ; cross-ref DQ-2, IP-4, GV-24/39 — **THE FIVE ECCLESIAL SACRAMENTS DO CONVEY GRACE — NON-SALVIFIC GRACE.** The grace half of the original Article 25 question, unanswered at DQ-2 and staged as Bucket C item 20, **was posted by JD on 2026-07-14 and answered by RJ on 2026-07-20, 11:20 PM** (Seven-sacraments thread), verbatim: *"I would submit that both are true: that they are generally accepted as appropriate parts in the Life of the Church, and that Grace is conveyed. This is not, of course, that salvific Grace that we see in Baptism and the Lord's Supper (the Romans would agree with us on that point), but rather the Grace of procreative unity, sanctification, etc."*

> **[Stated-Analysis]** He goes **beyond** the Homily's deflationary "general acception" — he affirms grace is genuinely conveyed — while holding the **salvific / non-salvific** line, which is the distinction that keeps him inside Article 25's "not of the same level and kind."
>
> **[Analysis] — RECOMMEND: LOG, DO NOT RE-OPEN.** There is a residual seam, and it is worth understanding even though it should not be run: **Article 25's stated ground** for the "have not like nature" verdict is *"for that they have not any visible sign or ceremony ordained of God"* — an **institution** ground, not a grace-quantum ground. RJ's answer distinguishes the five from the two by the *kind of grace conveyed*, which does not engage the Article's actual reason. But the Article 25 lever is **already retired to the do-not-deploy register** (DQ-2, formulary-faithful answer), and re-entering it on this narrow point would look like relitigating a question he answered well. **The residue is smaller than the goodwill it would cost.**
>
> **[Analysis] — factual flag, for JD's own knowledge, NOT for deployment.** His aside that *"the Romans would agree with us on that point"* is doubtful as stated. Trent (Sess. VII) holds all seven to be instituted by Christ and to confer grace *ex opere operato*; Rome distinguishes the sacraments by their *particular* sacramental grace, not by treating five of them as non-salvific in the sense he implies. **Correct for the record only.** Deploying it would spend real goodwill on a side point in a thread that has otherwise gone extremely well.

**DQ-7a.** [Stated] Anchor: §12 / §13 ; **discharges the two DQ-7 verification flags** — **DQ-7 VERIFIED AGAINST THE ARCHIVE; THE GREEK ARGUMENT AND THE TRENT HORN DIRECTION.** The DQ-7 fragments, previously logged as *"as relayed from the live thread"* with a standing verify-before-use flag, are now **checked against the archived post text (`SRC_Discord_RPW.md`, 2026-07-21, 11:42 AM) and confirmed verbatim-accurate.** ⚠️ **Both DQ-7 verification flags are DISCHARGED.** The full reply adds two things not previously logged:

What he draws from the passage instead: **(1)** saints pray, and "Saints are not limited to Heaven; St Paul calls people on earth Saints as well"; **(2)** "Their prayers are heard and offered in the Heavenly worship."
>

Correct the phrasing anywhere it appears: this is **RJ's own formulation**, which he reports Horn later adopting.
>

**DQ-12.** [Stated] ★★ Anchor: §2 (Scripture & Authority) / §Formularies ; cross-ref DQ-1, IP Article VI thread, GV-37 — **ARTICLE VI: HE CANNOT PRODUCE A REQUIRED-BUT-UNPROVABLE BELIEF, AND AFFIRMS MATERIAL SUFFICIENCY.** Asked (JD, 07-20 5:50 PM) for one or two concrete examples of the kind of belief a St Francis member would be expected to hold as part of the tradition *even though it isn't provable from Scripture*, RJ replied (Discord, **2026-07-21, 12:00 AM**). He first offered required use of the 1928 BCP liturgy, immediately hedging that "that might fall more into practice, though." Then, verbatim:

> *"The examples I keep coming up with fall more into the category of, 'I believe these are justified in light of the evidence of Scripture, but I do not think that a good-faith rejection of them is grounds for denying the salvation of someone.' So in one sense I would say these can be 'proved' from Scripture, just not necessarily to the satisfaction of all: 1) The invalidity of laymen celebrating the Lord's Supper. 2) The recognition of the threefold order: Bishop, Presbyter, and Deacon. 3) Various particular practices concerning worship (Feast Days, fasting days, etc; these largely culminate in the usage of the Book of Common Prayer)."*

> And the concession, in his own words: *"This is not quite what you are asking for, as I would say that I can prove (to my satisfaction) these things from Scripture. **I am having trouble thinking of particulars that fall in that 'can't be proved from Scripture, but we require it as part of our Tradition, but we don't say one is cut off from the Faith for rejecting' zone**, unless 'proved from Scripture' means, 'To the satisfaction of all rational people regardless of starting principles apart from a general recognition that **the Scriptures alone are infallible and materially sufficient for the essential doctrines of the Faith**.'"*
>
> **⚠️ [Analysis] — MAJOR, AND FAVOURABLE. The Article VI two-tier gloss collapses in his own hands.** The project's Article VI thread was probing a suspected two-tier structure: Scripture for salvation, tradition supplying further required beliefs. **He has now stated, unprompted and against his own interest, that he cannot populate the second tier.** Everything he can think of relocates into "provable from Scripture, though not to everyone's satisfaction," which is not a two-tier position at all — it is the ordinary Protestant position about the *perspicuity* of disputed inferences, and every confessional tradition holds something like it.
>
> **⚠️ [Analysis] — HE AFFIRMS MATERIAL SUFFICIENCY, IN HIS OWN WORDS.** *"The Scriptures alone are infallible and materially sufficient for the essential doctrines of the Faith."* This is a significant datum for the **broader `A Protestant Defense of the Reformation` workstream** as well as this project. **Log as common ground and credit it** (see §15). It forecloses a whole class of sola-scriptura arguments as inapplicable to him — which is a *gain*, not a loss: it means the disagreement is genuinely about application, not about the authority principle.
>
> **⚠️ [Analysis] — ITEM (3) IS THE FUNNEL PAYLOAD, AND IT ARRIVED FROM A DIFFERENT THREAD.** *"Various particular practices concerning worship (Feast Days, fasting days, etc.)"* are, on his own account, things he "can prove (to my satisfaction) from Scripture." **Incense is exactly such a practice.** So he has committed, generally and in a neutral context with incense nowhere in view, to the claim that **his distinctive worship practices are Scripturally provable.** That is the **DQ-4 warrant rule restated in the practice register, independently reconfirmed from a second thread.** It licenses the friendliest possible framing of the eventual incense question: *"You mentioned that the particular worship practices are ones you take to be provable from Scripture. Could you walk me through the proof on one of them?"* — an invitation to teach, not a challenge to defend.
>
> **[Analysis] — JD's 07-21 10:15 AM close was well judged.** It banks the concession on the record in RJ's hearing, without pressing, and it credits the material-sufficiency affirmation explicitly. **No further move is needed in that thread.** The DQ-1 closure question (below) is the only thing still owed there, and it is now largely moot.

**DQ-13.** [Stated] Anchor: §7 (Baptism) ; cross-ref the WCF 28.6 OQ, D6, Q6, Q9, GV-4/23/26 — **BAPTISM AND CONFIRMATION (thread opened by another parishioner, not JD).** In a thread started by *LilleyPartyofFive* with follow-ups from *chrissy smith* and *Karis*, RJ gave a short answer (**2026-06-30, 12:56 PM**) and a full one (**2026-07-04, 2:23 AM**). Short answer: Confirmation's roots are "the laying on of hands by the Apostles in Acts"; **"One is not going from not having the Holy Ghost to having the Holy Ghost; rather, one is receiving a strengthening of the Holy Ghost"**; "The Bishop is the only one who can Confirm, in the Anglican Tradition." In a separate one-line message: **"We objectively receive the Holy Ghost at Baptism."** Full answer: **"Baptism is the receiving of the Holy Ghost (Acts 2:38), whereas in Confirmation we receive a 'stirring up' or 'filling' of the Holy Ghost,"** argued from John 20:21-22 vs. Acts 2:1-4, Acts 2:38 vs. Acts 8:14-17, and 2 Tim 1:6-7; Acts 8 read as God "emphasizing the universality of the Gospel and Descent of the Holy Ghost successively, as ripples from a tossed stone." An **act-level** account of what constitutes an act of worship, from his own mouth, in a context with no polemical stake, sitting against DQ-9's principle-level substitution. **(b)** *The object carries the worship* — what made it worship was the pagan altar and the false god, so the act-level reading proves nothing about incense as such.
⚠️ **Reading (b) is strong and is very likely what he would say. Do not log (a) as though it were established.** ⚠️ **He is describing pagan practice and says nothing whatever about Christian liturgical incense in this session.** The value is that the datum is his, requires no contested Reformed premise, and is portable.

### ⚠️⚠️ READ BEFORE USING ANY FINDING IN THIS LEDGER

**1. ⛔ EVERY FINDING HERE IS THEN-SIDE BY CONSTRUCTION, AND THIS IS THE FIRST FACT ABOUT THE BATCH.** The six sources run **2018-07-01 to 2020-04-30**. Rev. **BLOG-52.** [Stated] Anchor: §2 Scripture & Authority ; cross-ref RC4-1, RC4-3, RC4-4, RC4-6, RC4-7, RC4-2, DQ-1 — ⭐⭐⭐ **THE DEUTEROCANON POSITION, WHOLE, IN 2016 — AND IT IS THE `RC-4` POSITION TEN YEARS EARLY.** He prefers **"Deuterocanon"** to **"Apocrypha"** and says so explicitly, calling it the better name. Circumcision logged as the reserve analogy. **Downstream pointers recorded** to `RJ_Incense_Analysis.md` §4.12 (with §10.4 reordered to lead with the priesthood argument, all four rebuttals retained) and to staged question **1e / `Q-Inc-5`**, which is **filed and not posted**. **Live state untouched: DQ-5 remains OUTSTANDING, the DQ-7 Revelation strand remains ANSWERED BUT UNGROUNDED and not closed, and the pending Discord turn is unchanged.** **Purpose header added** recording audience, class, function, and handling, including the standing rules that the three-layer attribution system may never be flattened, that verbatim quotes are byte-offset verified before logging, and that external commentary is logged as [Analysis] and never given a source tag. Per JD: em/en-dash policing skipped this pass.
